0.1 What this handbook is

This is the single operating manual for the Data Analytics & BI department. It does two jobs at once: it trains a beginner into a professional analytics engineer, and it defines the corporate process used to deliver analytics projects to clients, including international clients, from the first enquiry (0%) to a signed-off, maintained solution (100%).

Nothing here assumes you already know the subject. Every technical word is explained the first time it appears. Where a number depends on a vendor price or a law, this handbook tells you to verify it from the official source on the day you quote instead of printing a figure that will go out of date.

Honest scope note

A 90-day plan can take a motivated beginner to supervised junior-analyst level across Levels 1–5, with a working introduction to Levels 6–7. It cannot produce an independent senior engineer; that takes roughly 6–12 months of real project work. This handbook plans for that reality instead of promising otherwise.

0.3 The twelve golden rules of the department

  1. Never assume the client's data is correct. Audit it first (Stage 04). Every project starts with a data-quality assessment.
  2. Sell business outcomes, not charts. A dashboard is a means; a trusted, verified management report is the product.
  3. One definition per KPI. If two people calculate "revenue" differently, the dashboard is wrong even if the maths is right.
  4. Reconcile before you publish. Important numbers must match a trusted source record, with evidence saved.
  5. Never commit client data, personal data, passwords or API keys to Git. Not once, not temporarily.
  6. Predictions are estimates, not promises. Always show a baseline, the error, and the limitations.
  7. Choose the simplest tool that works. Excel before Power BI, a SQL view before a pipeline, a chart before a model.
  8. Write it down. If it is not in a document or ticket, it did not happen.
  9. Do not move forward until the previous level is understood. Gates are real; a failed gate means repeat, not skip.
  10. Small steps, saved often. Commit whenever something works; keep every transformation reproducible.
  11. Ask early. Being stuck for 30 minutes without asking is a mistake, not a virtue.
  12. Client data belongs to the client. Treat it as if it were your own bank details; use the minimum needed, for the agreed purpose only.

0.4 How to use the handbook day to day

  1. Find today's week in the 90-day schedule (Part 5). Read the week's objectives before touching a tool.
  2. Follow the 15-step teaching format (Part 8) for each topic. Do the practical assignment, not just the reading.
  3. Save every deliverable in the named folder. Update your daily log (template in Annex B).
  4. At the end of each level, take the gate assessment. Pass mark and rules are in Part 4.
  5. If anything in this book is wrong, unclear or out of date, tell the Head of Data & Analytics; they will fix the book. Improving it is part of everyone's job.

Part 1 — Department Charter and Commercial Services

1.1 Mission

To turn clients' scattered, unverified business data into trusted decisions: one verified reporting environment per client, delivered on time, documented, secure, and maintained on a monthly service.

LineWhat the client receivesTypical outputsRecurring revenue?
A. Data AnalyticsAnswers to business questions: where is revenue leaking, who are our best customers, why did margin fall?Analysis report, KPI pack, customer segments, trend and root-cause findingsSometimes (retainer)

1.3 Selling outcomes, not dashboards

Do not sellSell instead
"A Power BI dashboard""A management reporting solution that consolidates sales, finance and operations data into one verified reporting environment, so the owner sees the same numbers as the accountant."
"A churn model""An early-warning list of customers likely to leave next quarter, so the account team can act, measured against what happens without the model."
"ETL pipelines""Reports that refresh themselves every morning, so nobody spends two days a month copying Excel sheets."

Regulated industries

Healthcare and finance data carry legal duties (for example India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, and for overseas clients GDPR or HIPAA). Never accept a regulated-data project until the Founder and the client's data owner have agreed the legal basis, storage location and access rules in writing. When unsure, escalate; do not decide alone.

Power BI on Mac or Linux

Power BI Desktop runs on Windows only. A trainee on another system uses a company Windows virtual machine or loaner laptop for Weeks 8–9. Plan this in advance; check Microsoft Learn for current options.

Python project environment (do this once per project)

# Windows (PowerShell)
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install pandas numpy matplotlib openpyxl requests

# Linux / macOS
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install pandas numpy matplotlib openpyxl requests

# Record exactly what you installed, so the next person can repeat it
pip freeze > requirements.txt

Why a virtual environment? It keeps each project's libraries separate, so upgrading one project never breaks another. Common error: "python is not recognised" means Python was installed without "Add python.exe to PATH"; re-run the installer and tick that box.

Part 4 — Training Roadmap: Levels 1 to 7

Seven levels, taught strictly in order. Each level ends with a gate: a written test and a practical task marked against a rubric. Do not start the next level until the gate is passed.

LevelTopics (all taught from zero)HoursProof of learning
1 Data FundamentalsWhat is data; structured, semi-structured, unstructured; databases vs spreadsheets; tables, rows, columns; data types; primary and foreign keys; data quality; data lifecycle; business KPIs; data governance25Assignment A1 (data audit) + quiz
2 ExcelEntry and formatting; sorting, filtering; IF, SUMIF, COUNTIF; XLOOKUP; PivotTables; charts; data validation; Power Query; dashboard basics45Project 1: Excel business dashboard
3 SQLDatabase basics; SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE; WHERE, ORDER BY; GROUP BY, HAVING; JOINs; subqueries; CTEs; window functions; views; indexes; optimisation; database security55Project 2: SQL sales analysis (30 queries)
4 PythonFundamentals; variables, lists, dicts; functions; file handling; pandas; NumPy; Matplotlib; cleaning; transformation; API extraction; error handling; automated reporting60Project 3: cleaning project with tests
5 Business IntelligencePower BI Desktop; Power Query; data modelling; relationships; DAX; measures vs calculated columns; dashboard design; filters; row-level security; scheduled refresh; Power BI Service; Tableau fundamentals and alternatives60Project 4: executive dashboard
6 Data EngineeringETL vs ELT; pipelines; API integration; PostgreSQL; warehouses; star and snowflake schemas; fact and dimension tables; incremental loading; validation; scheduling; failure handling55Projects 5 and 6: API-to-DB pipeline; automated monthly report
7 Predictive AnalyticsStatistics; probability; correlation; regression; classification; time-series; clustering; feature engineering; evaluation; overfitting; data leakage; monitoring; when NOT to predict50Project 7: forecast vs baseline; then Project 8

Hours are guided learning plus practice. Add review and assessment time. Total about 350 hours, or about 9 weeks of full-time study; the rest of the 13 weeks is projects, gates, revision and client-process training.

4.1 Gate rules

  • Written test: pass mark 70%. Open-book for syntax, closed-book for concepts.
  • Practical task: rubric of 5 lines scored 0–5. Every line must score 3 or more and the average must be 3.5 or more.
  • Fail: mentor writes a gap list; trainee repeats only the weak topics for up to one week; one retake. A second failure triggers a mentor and Founder review of the plan.
  • Assessors mark the evidence (files, queries, screenshots) not the explanation given in person.

4.2 When predictive analytics is appropriate, and when it is not

Predictive work is the most over-sold service in analytics. Use this decision table before proposing it:

QuestionIf yesIf no
Is there a clear decision that a prediction will change? (e.g. order more stock, call a customer)ContinueDo a dashboard or analysis instead
Is there enough clean history? (guide: at least 2 full seasonal cycles for forecasting; hundreds of examples of the rare class for classification)ContinueCollect data first; offer descriptive analytics now
Can a simple baseline (last year's value, moving average, average rate) be beaten by a clear margin?Model is justifiedUse the baseline and say so honestly
Will the pattern stay stable? (not disrupted by price changes, new products, one-off events)ContinueWarn the client; add monitoring and shorter horizons
Can the client act on it and measure the result?Deploy after approvalDo not deploy; document findings only

Never promise outcomes

Predictions are probabilistic estimates with error. Every deliverable must show the baseline, the error measure on unseen data, the assumptions, and the sentence: "Forecasts are estimates and not guaranteed outcomes."

5.1 Daily habits that make the plan work

  • Daily log (template in Annex B): what I did, what I learned, what blocked me, what is next. Five lines, no more.
  • Commit every day: at least one commit with a clear message. Message format: L3.05: add window-function queries (level.task: message).
  • Explain it aloud: end each topic by explaining it to your buddy in two minutes. If you cannot, you do not yet understand it.
  • Break it on purpose: after something works, change an input and see how it fails. This is how errors become familiar, not frightening.

5.2 Weekly review (Friday, 45 minutes, mentor)

  1. Show the week's deliverable running, not slides.
  2. Mentor asks three "why" questions about the work; answers are noted.
  3. Defects found are logged with owner and fix date.
  4. Plan for next week confirmed; any slippage handled by cutting scope, not by skipping tests.

6.2 How to choose tools for a client

Choose by evidence, in this order, and write the reasons into the architecture document (Stage 05):

FactorQuestion to ask the clientEffect on choice
Existing ecosystemDo they already use Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, or neither?Microsoft 365 users: Power BI is natural. Google-centric: Looker Studio is strong and cheap.
BudgetWhat can they spend per month on licences and cloud?Low budget: Excel + Looker Studio + PostgreSQL. Verify licence prices on the day you quote.
Data volumeRows per table now and in 2 years? Refresh frequency?Under a few million rows: PostgreSQL is enough. Tens of millions and growing: consider a cloud warehouse.
UsersHow many viewers and creators? Mobile? External sharing?Per-user licences scale with viewers; check Power BI licensing rules for sharing and capacity.
LicensingIs any tool restricted by their policy or by data-residency law?Record licence terms; open-source preferred where equal.
MaintenanceWho looks after it after handover? Skills they have?Prefer fewer moving parts; a simple stack the client can own beats a clever one only VEL can run.
SecuritySensitive data? Required hosting region? Audit needs?May force on-premises or a specific cloud region, and row-level security.

Verify before quoting

Vendor prices, licence tiers and free-tier limits change often. Before any proposal, open the vendor's official pricing page, record the date, URL and the plan name in the cost sheet, and attach a screenshot. Never copy a price from memory, a blog or this handbook.

6.3 Reference architecture (default)

Each arrow is a logged, repeatable step. Raw data is never edited; fixes are made in the clean layer so you can always trace a dashboard number back to the original record (data lineage).

Hard stops

No Stage 05 before Stage 04 is complete. No Stage 15 without written production approval. No client dataset leaves the approved environment at any stage. No dashboard is published until key metrics are reconciled (Stage 14).

Part 9 — Commercial Model and Pricing

9.1 The formulas

Total Project Cost = Labour + Software licences + Infrastructure + Data engineering + Dashboard development + QA + Project management + Other direct costs. (Labour is the hours of each role at that role's fully loaded cost rate; listing engineering, dashboard, QA and PM separately keeps the estimate auditable.)

Selling price = (Delivery cost + Risk contingency + Overhead) / (1 − Target profit margin).

Gross margin = (Price − Direct delivery cost) / Price.   Break-even (monthly) = Fixed monthly overhead / Contribution per recurring contract, where contribution = monthly fee − monthly cost to serve.

9.2 Worked example (ILLUSTRATIVE numbers, not VEL rates)

Small retail client, one executive dashboard, three data sources, one nightly pipeline. Rates and percentages below are assumptions chosen to show the arithmetic; replace them with VEL's approved rate card and verified vendor prices.

Risk contingency 15%31,590
Overhead 20% of (cost + contingency)48,438
Full cost2,90,628
Price at 30% target margin: 2,90,628 / 0.704,15,183 (quote INR 4,15,000)

Check: gross margin = (4,15,000 − 2,10,600) / 4,15,000 = 49.3%. If the contingency is fully used, profit is 4,15,000 − 2,90,628 = INR 1,24,372, a net margin of 30.0%.

Also compute and record for each project: cost per dashboard (dashboard development + its share of QA and PM / number of dashboards), cost per pipeline, cost per customer (total delivery and support cost / active clients), recurring revenue (sum of monthly fees) and licence and cloud expenses as separate lines.

Part 12 — First Practical Assignment (A1): Audit a Sales Dataset

Level 1 · Week 1 · Estimated time 6–8 hours · Data: synthetic (generated by the script below)

This assignment follows the 15-step teaching format (Part 8.1). It is deliberately small: the aim is to learn to distrust data politely and to prove, with evidence, what is wrong with it. This is Stage 04 in miniature.

1. Definition

A data audit is a systematic, read-only inspection of a dataset to find missing values, duplicates, wrong formats, impossible values and inconsistent definitions, before anyone builds a report on it.

2. Business purpose

A dashboard built on unaudited data shows confident wrong numbers. The audit is the cheapest place to find errors and the first thing a client sees that proves VEL is careful.

3. Real-world example

"Sunrise Retail" (fictional) exports 505 order lines from its billing software. The owner says January–June sales were "about right". Before building anything we check: are there duplicate orders (double counting revenue)? Negative quantities? Dates in two formats (so some months sort wrongly)? Regions typed in different cases (so a pivot shows "north" and "North" as two regions)? Each defect changes the totals.

4–6. Software, installation and configuration

  • Python 3.11+, pandas, VS Code, Git (Part 3.5). Excel or Google Sheets for the manual check.
  • Create the folder a1-sales-audit/, create and activate a virtual environment, run pip install pandas, then save the two scripts below into the folder.
  • Use git init and add a .gitignore (Part 8.3). Even though this data is fake, practise the habit.

7. Step-by-step implementation

  1. Run generate_sales_data.py. It writes data/sales_raw.csv (505 rows). The fixed seed 2505 means everybody gets the same file.
  2. Open the CSV in Excel. Without code, write down by eye 3 problems you can spot. (Most are hidden; this shows why code is needed.)
  3. Read audit_data.py line by line. For each of the six checks write one sentence: what does it test and why does it matter?
  4. Run the audit script. Compare its numbers with your Excel observations.
  5. Reproduce two of the checks in Excel: remove duplicates (note the count), and add a helper column =F2*G2-H2 to find revenue mismatches.
  6. Write the audit report (template in Annex A): findings table, business impact of each, recommended fix, and the question you would ask the data owner.
  7. Commit with the message L1.01: audit sales_raw.csv and report findings.

8. Code

generate_sales_data.py (creates synthetic data with deliberate defects)

"""Generate the synthetic 'Sunrise Retail' sales dataset for Assignment A1.

All data is fake. A fixed seed makes the output identical on every machine.
Deliberate defects are injected so the trainee can practise a data audit.
"""
import csv
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

SEED = 2505
N_ROWS = 500
OUT = Path(__file__).parent / "data" / "sales_raw.csv"

REGIONS = ["North", "South", "East", "West"]
PRODUCTS = {"P01": ("Notebook", 120.0), "P02": ("Pen Pack", 60.0),
            "P03": ("Backpack", 850.0), "P04": ("Desk Lamp", 640.0),
            "P05": ("Water Bottle", 310.0)}


def build_rows(rng: random.Random) -> list[dict]:
    start = date(2025, 1, 1)
    rows = []
    for i in range(1, N_ROWS + 1):
        pid = rng.choice(list(PRODUCTS))
        qty = rng.randint(1, 10)
        price = PRODUCTS[pid][1]
        rows.append({
            "order_id": f"ORD{i:04d}",
            "order_date": (start + timedelta(days=rng.randint(0, 179))).isoformat(),
            "customer_id": f"C{rng.randint(1, 80):03d}",
            "region": rng.choice(REGIONS),
            "product_id": pid,
            "quantity": qty,
            "unit_price": price,
            "revenue": round(qty * price, 2),
        })
    return rows


def inject_defects(rows: list[dict], rng: random.Random) -> None:
    """Break the data on purpose (about 4% of rows)."""
    for r in rng.sample(rows, 10):
        r["region"] = ""                       # missing value
    for r in rng.sample(rows, 8):
        r["region"] = r["region"].lower() or "north"  # inconsistent case
    for r in rng.sample(rows, 5):
        r["quantity"] = -abs(int(r["quantity"]))      # impossible value
    for r in rng.sample(rows, 6):
        d = date.fromisoformat(r["order_date"])
        r["order_date"] = d.strftime("%d/%m/%Y")      # wrong date format
    for r in rng.sample(rows, 4):
        r["revenue"] = round(float(r["revenue"]) * 1.5, 2)  # wrong calculation
    rows.extend(dict(r) for r in rng.sample(rows, 5))        # duplicate rows


def main() -> None:
    rng = random.Random(SEED)
    rows = build_rows(rng)
    inject_defects(rows, rng)
    OUT.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with OUT.open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"Wrote {len(rows)} rows to {OUT}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

audit_data.py (read-only audit; never changes the source file)

"""Data-quality audit for sales_raw.csv (Stage 04 practice).

Usage:  python audit_data.py [path/to/file.csv]
Read-only: never edits the source file.
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

path = Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else Path(__file__).parent / "data" / "sales_raw.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(path, dtype=str, keep_default_na=False)   # read everything as text first

print(f"File: {path.name}")
print(f"Rows: {len(df)}   Columns: {len(df.columns)}")

blank = {c: int((df[c].str.strip() == "").sum()) for c in df.columns}
print("\n1. Missing values (blank cells):")
for c, n in blank.items():
    if n:
        print(f"   {c}: {n}")

print(f"\n2. Fully duplicated rows: {int(df.duplicated().sum())}")
print(f"   Duplicate order_id values: {int(df['order_id'].duplicated().sum())}")

dates = pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
print(f"\n3. order_date not in YYYY-MM-DD format: {int(dates.isna().sum())}")

qty = pd.to_numeric(df["quantity"], errors="coerce")
print(f"\n4. quantity <= 0: {int((qty <= 0).sum())}")

reg = df.loc[df["region"].str.strip() != "", "region"]
bad_case = int((reg != reg.str.title()).sum())
print(f"\n5. region values with inconsistent case: {bad_case}")

calc = (qty * pd.to_numeric(df["unit_price"], errors="coerce")).round(2)
mismatch = int((calc != pd.to_numeric(df["revenue"], errors="coerce")).sum())
print(f"\n6. revenue != quantity x unit_price: {mismatch}")

print("\nVerdict: DO NOT use for reporting until defects are resolved with the data owner.")

9. Expected output

Run on the file above, the real output of the audit script is:

File: sales_raw.csv
Rows: 505   Columns: 8

1. Missing values (blank cells):
   region: 10

2. Fully duplicated rows: 5
   Duplicate order_id values: 5

3. order_date not in YYYY-MM-DD format: 6

4. quantity <= 0: 5

5. region values with inconsistent case: 8

6. revenue != quantity x unit_price: 9

Verdict: DO NOT use for reporting until defects are resolved with the data owner.

The first rows of sales_raw.csv start with: ORD0001, 2025-06-05, C066, North, P03, 8, 850.0, 6800.0.

10. Verification

CheckHow to prove itExpected
Row countlen(df) or Excel status bar505 data rows (500 orders + 5 duplicates)
DuplicatesExcel: Data > Remove Duplicates (all columns)5 rows removed
Missing regionExcel filter on blanks10 rows
Revenue mismatchHelper column =F2*G2-H29 non-zero rows
Why 9, not the 4 injected?Inspect the mismatching rows4 rows had revenue inflated by 1.5x, and the 5 rows given a negative quantity no longer equal quantity x price, so both defect groups show up

11. Common errors

Message or symptomCauseFix
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'Virtual environment not active or pandas not installedActivate .venv, run pip install pandas
FileNotFoundError ... sales_raw.csvGenerator not run, or run from another folderRun the generator first; the scripts use paths relative to their own folder

Counts differ from this bookA different seed or edited fileRe-generate with seed 2505; do not edit the CSV

12. Security considerations

  • Treat the file as if it were real client data: do not email it or upload it to online tools.
  • The audit is read-only. Never overwrite the raw file; later cleaning writes a new file in data/processed/.
  • Real projects: a data-sharing agreement must exist before any file is received (Stage 02).

13. Documentation

Create README.md (what the project is, how to run both scripts) and docs/data-dictionary.md with one row per column: name, meaning, type, allowed values, and known issues. For example: region — text — North/South/East/West — 10 blanks, 8 wrong-case.

14. Practical assignment (deliverables)

  1. audit_report.md or PDF (Annex A template), maximum 2 pages.
  2. Both scripts, plus README and data dictionary, committed to Git.
  3. Extension (required): add two new checks to audit_data.py — (a) customer_id values not matching the pattern C### and (b) order_date values later than today — and explain what results you get.
  4. A 2-minute spoken explanation to your buddy of why raw data must not be edited.

15. Assessment

Rubric line5 = excellent3 = pass0 = fail
Completeness of findingsAll six defect types found with countsAt least five typesFewer than four
EvidenceEvery finding backed by query output or screenshotMost backedStatements without evidence
Business impactEach defect tied to a wrong number or decisionImpact stated for mostNone
Safe handlingRaw file untouched; Git history cleanMinor slip, correctedRaw file edited
DocumentationREADME and dictionary allow a stranger to repeat the workUnderstandable with gapsMissing

Pass: every line 3 or more, average 3.5 or more, and Quiz Q1 (Annex C) at 70% or higher. Do not start Level 2 until A1 is passed.

Annex C — Quiz Q1 (Level 1, Week 1) and Trainer Answer Key

Trainer copy. Trainees receive the questions only. Pass mark 7 of 10.

#QuestionAnswer key
1Give one example each of structured, semi-structured and unstructured data.Structured: sales table. Semi-structured: JSON from an API. Unstructured: customer email text, images.
2What is a primary key, and why must it be unique and not blank?Column(s) that identify one row; duplicates or blanks make rows ambiguous and break joins.
3What is a foreign key? Give an example.A column referencing another table's primary key, e.g. sales.customer_id to customers.customer_id.
4Name four data quality dimensions and test one for sales_raw.csv.Completeness, uniqueness, validity, consistency, accuracy, timeliness. E.g. completeness: 10 blank regions.
5Why do we never edit raw data?Traceability and repeatability; fixes happen in a clean layer so every number can be traced back.
6Define KPI and give a good and a bad example.A measurable value tied to a goal. Good: monthly revenue by region, defined precisely. Bad: "sales" with no definition or period.
7A row has quantity -3. List two possible explanations and what to do.Return/credit note or entry error. Do not guess; ask the owner and document the rule.
8What is data governance in one sentence?Agreed ownership, rules, quality standards and access controls for data.
9Why is it unsafe to put a database password in a Git repository?History keeps it forever and others can read it; use environment variables or a password manager.
10Name the stages of the data lifecycle.Collect, store, process/clean, analyse, share/report, retain/archive, delete.
